R1. READ THE REGISTRY'S READER BEFORE ADDING TO IT (PO-6 again, and it paid
    twice). Adding tools/bm_bbstatus.py to the network allow-list turned
    test_bm.py red on the PACKAGING gate, because pyproject.toml decides what
    a pip install receives and a new module absent from py-modules ships
    broken. Adding the two new suites turned test_all.py's inventory gate red
    until CI had a step for each. Both refusals are the controls working, and
    both were cheaper than the failure they prevent.

R2. A CONTROL THAT READS A COMMAND STRING BREAKS WHEN THE COMMAND CHANGES
    SHAPE. Four separate controls read hook program names out of the raw
    command text. Moving the chains into one table meant teaching all four to
    read the table, and the floors they enforce did NOT move (8 command
    strings, 12 programs), which is the test of whether a refactor kept its
    coverage. If a count has to be lowered to stay green, the coverage moved,
    and lowering it is the wrong fix.

R3. WHEN A PLAN ARRIVES FROM OUTSIDE, CHECK IT CLAIM BY CLAIM. The Bitbucket
    remediation plan named two real defects here, two things that were
    already true, and a set of items that belong to the sibling's assurance
    kernel, which this repository does not contain. Building half a provider
    contract here would have created exactly the false compatibility the plan
    warns about. The verdicts are in docs/BITBUCKET.md as a table, including
    the FALSE ones, so the next reader does not re-litigate them.

R4. THE GATE NEEDS A COMMITTED TREE. The first branch battery was launched
    with everything STAGED, and test_all's clean-checkout check reads `git
    status --porcelain`, where a staged addition is dirt. It would have
    reported "the suites modified tracked files" and blamed the suites for
    the session's own staging. Killed by PID after printing the target (never
    pkill -f), committed, re-run.
